title: Paper Shape Coin Lab
subject: science
learningGoal: Test which folded paper shape holds the most weight, and keep the test fair.
realWorldHook: Bridges and buildings use columns. Engineers test which shapes are strongest before they build.

materials.householdSubstitution: Any matching printer paper, magazine pages or used envelopes
A paper clip or a little glue
Large lego bricks, small books or wooden blocks

noPurchaseRoute: Use any three matching sheets of paper and anything small and stackable you already have; coins are optional.
parentPreview: Your child folds the same paper into a tube, a triangle and a square column, guesses which will hold the most, then tests by stacking coins or blocks on a small book placed on top. You help keep the test fair: same paper, same height, same way of adding weight.

parent.parentSays: Bridges stand on columns. If we fold paper into different shapes, which do you think can hold the most?
parent.whyThisWorks: A prediction gives your child something to check, which is the heart of an experiment.

child.screen: Which paper shape is the strongest?
child.readAloudText: Which paper shape is the strongest? Tap I'm ready.

parent.parentSays: We'll make a tube, a triangle and a square. Which one do you predict will hold the most?
parent.whyThisWorks: There's no wrong guess. We record it so we can compare it with what happens.

child.screen: Guess! Which shape will hold the most?
child.readAloudText: Guess which shape will hold the most.

parent.parentSays: Fold each sheet into its shape and tape it. Make them the same height so it's fair.
parent.whyThisWorks: Same paper and same height means only the shape changes. That's a fair test.

child.screen: Fold and tape three shapes. Make them the same height.
child.readAloudText: Fold and tape three shapes, all the same height.

parent.parentSays: Stand one shape up, put a small book on top, and add coins one at a time until it squashes. Count how many it held.
parent.whyThisWorks: Adding one at a time and counting makes the result a number you can compare.

child.screen: Add coins one at a time. How many did the tube hold?
child.readAloudText: Add coins one at a time. Count until it squashes.

parent.parentSays: Which shape held the most? Why do you think it was stronger?
parent.whyThisWorks: Tubes spread weight all the way around with no weak corners. Your child doesn't need the word; noticing is enough.

child.screen: Which shape won? Tell your grown-up why.

parent.parentSays: Ask the two check questions below. Give your child time to think, then note how each one went.
Were you surprised? Where have you seen round columns in real life?

expectedResponses: The tube usually holds the most
Fair test: same paper, same height, add weight the same way

misconceptions.signal: Makes shapes different heights or uses different paper, or presses down.
misconceptions.supportiveNextQuestion: If one column is taller, can we tell whether the shape or the height made the difference?

misconceptions.signal: Drops several coins at once or pushes the book.
misconceptions.supportiveNextQuestion: What could happen if we drop lots at once? How can we make each try the same?

misconceptions.signal: Upset that the guess didn't match, or changes the guess afterwards.
misconceptions.supportiveNextQuestion: Scientists are often surprised. What did we learn because our guess was different?

checkQuestions.parentAsks: If we tested again, what must stay the same to be fair?

interpretation.clear: Names at least one: same paper, same height, same way of adding weight.
interpretation.not_yet: Suggests changing several things at once.

child.screen: To make it fair, what stays the same?
child.readAloudText: To make it fair, what should stay the same?

checkQuestions.parentAsks: Where in real life do you see round columns holding things up?

interpretation.clear: Gives an example (pillars, table legs, tree trunks, cans) and links it to the test.
interpretation.partial: Gives an example but can't link it.

child.screen: Where do you see strong round shapes holding things up?
child.readAloudText: Where do you see strong round shapes holding things up? Tell your grown-up.

extension: Try the tube with paper twice as thick (two sheets). Does doubling the paper double the coins?

shorterVersion.description: Build only a tube and a square and compare those two.

accessibilityAdaptations: You do the folding and taping; your child adds weight and counts.
Use large blocks instead of coins for easier handling.

hazards: Coins and small items are a choking hazard
Collapsing stacks may slide off the table
safety.supervision: An adult stays at the table the whole time. Coins and other small items are a choking hazard. Keep them away from younger siblings and use larger counters (blocks, bottle caps glued in pairs, or folded paper squares) if anyone in the room is under 3.
stopConditions: Anyone puts a coin in their mouth
A younger sibling comes near the small items
The stack becomes taller than the child's shoulders
safety.cleanup: Count the coins back into a container so none are left on the floor; recycle the paper.

optionalKit.description: A starter kit with card strips and large counters. Optional: everything here works with household items.
